pythagoras.name: Pythagoras of Samos
pythagoras.role: Founder of Pythagorean philosophy & mathematical science
pythagoras.summary: Honored by Nicomachus (I.1.1) as the first to define philosophy as the 'love of wisdom' (φιλοσοφία), restricting wisdom to the exact science of eternal, immaterial realities accessible through the four mathemata.

philolaus.name: Philolaus of Croton
philolaus.summary: Formulated the metaphysics of Limit and Unlimited; called the cube 'geometric harmony' (γεωμετρικὴ ἁρμονία) because its 6 faces, 8 vertices, and 12 edges embody the harmonic mean (II.26.2, II.29).

archytas.name: Archytas of Tarentum
archytas.summary: Quoted verbatim by Nicomachus in Book I, Ch. 3.4 ('For these sciences seem to be sisters': arithmetic, geometry, sphaerics, and music); defined the three classical means (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic, originally 'subcontrary') and proved no rational mean exists in a superparticular ratio.

androcydes.name: Androcydes the Pythagorean
androcydes.summary: Cited by Nicomachus (I.3.3) alongside Eubulides, Aristoxenus, Hippobotus, and Neanthes as confirming the Pythagorean fourfold curriculum of quantity and magnitude.

plato.name: Plato of Athens
plato.summary: Repeatedly invoked by Nicomachus: Timaeus 27d (Being vs. flux, I.2), Republic VII 527d–533d ('eye of the soul' & 'steps and bridges' of the mathemata, I.3.5–7), Epinomis 991d–992a ('bond of all these', I.3.5), Timaeus 35a–36b (Same & Other and World-Soul scale, II.18 & II.29), and the Nuptial Number (Republic VIII 546b–c, II.24).

eudoxus.name: Eudoxus of Cnidus
eudoxus.summary: Credited in ancient mathematical history (Iamblichus on Nicomachus II.28) with adding the 4th, 5th, and 6th subcontrary means to the three archaic Pythagorean means.

aristotle.name: Aristotle of Stagira
aristotle.summary: Distinguished discrete and continuous quantity in Categories 6 (4b20) and formulated the principle of ontological priority by non-reciprocal elimination (συναναιρεῖ μὲν, οὐ συναναιρεῖται δέ) deployed by Nicomachus in I.4–5 to rank the Quadrivium.

euclid.name: Euclid of Alexandria
euclid.summary: Demonstrated the dyadic sufficiency theorem for even perfect numbers in Elements IX.36 and foundational number theory across Books VII–IX using line-segment diagrams, contrasted with Nicomachus's inductive α-pebble and tabular style.
euclid.hoche_loci: I.11–16 (cf. Elem. VII & IX.36), II.21–27 (cf. Elem. V & VI.13)

eratosthenes.name: Eratosthenes of Cyrene
eratosthenes.summary: Inventor of the Sieve (κόσκινον, preserved solely in its odd-only form by Nicomachus I.13) AND documented in Iamblichus/Pappus for deriving all ratios from Equality via the three-term rule expounded by Nicomachus in I.23.

myonides.name: Myonides & Euphranor
myonides.summary: Credited by Iamblichus (In Nicomachi Arith. Introd.) with introducing the four later Neo-Pythagorean means (Means 7–10) catalogued by Nicomachus in Book II, Ch. 28.

nicomachus.name: Nicomachus of Gerasa
nicomachus.summary: Born at Gerasa in the Syrian Decapolis; author of the Introductio Arithmetica (Books I–II), the Enchiridion Harmonices, and the lost Theologumena Arithmeticae. His treatise served via Boethius as the universal textbook of arithmetic for a thousand years.

theon-of-smyrna.name: Theon of Smyrna
theon-of-smyrna.summary: Contemporary of Nicomachus and author of Mathematics Useful for Understanding Plato, preserving parallel accounts of side-and-diagonal numbers, figurate gnomons, and the derivation of ratios from equality.

apuleius.name: Apuleius of Madauros
apuleius.role: Latin Platonist & first translator of Nicomachus
apuleius.summary: Composed the earliest (now lost) Latin translation of Nicomachus's Introductio Arithmetica within a single generation of its composition, as attested by Cassiodorus and Isidore of Seville.

iamblichus.name: Iamblichus of Chalcis
iamblichus.summary: Elevated Nicomachus's Introductio to Book IV of his ten-book Collection of Pythagorean Doctrines (In Nicomachi Arithmeticam Introductionem, ed. Pistelli 1894), recording the history of the Ten Means.

pappus.name: Pappus of Alexandria
pappus.summary: In Synagoge Book III (Props. 12–27), constructs all three classical means in a single semicircle and systematically analyzes the Ten Nicomachean Means (`geometor/pappus`).

proclus.name: Proclus Lycius Diadochus
proclus.role: Head of the Athenian Academy; reported in tradition as Nicomachus reborn
proclus.summary: Marinus's Vita Procli (§28) records that Proclus believed his own soul belonged to the Pythagorean chain of Nicomachus of Gerasa; his Euclid Prologue (`geometor/proclus`, Friedlein 35–37) adopts Nicomachus's exact division of the Quadrivium.

philoponus.name: John Philoponus
philoponus.summary: Authored the largest surviving Greek scholia/commentary on both books of Nicomachus (ed. Richard Hoche, 1864–1867), derived from the Alexandrian lectures of Ammonius Hermeiou.

boethius.name: Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius
boethius.role: Roman statesman, philosopher & Latin adapter of Nicomachus
boethius.summary: Adapted Nicomachus into De Institutione Arithmetica (ed. Friedlein 1867) and De Institutione Musica, coining the enduring Latin word quadrivium ('fourfold path', De Inst. Arith. I.1) directly rendering Nicomachus I.3–4.
boethius.hoche_loci: De Inst. Arith. I–II (paralleling Nicomachus I–II)

aquinas.name: Thomas Aquinas
aquinas.summary: Received Nicomachean discrete-vs.-continuous quantity, relative ratio, and the hierarchy of the Quadrivium through Boethius in his Commentary on Boethius's De Trinitate (`geometor/aquinas`).

fibonacci.name: Leonardo Pisano (Fibonacci)
fibonacci.role: Author of Liber Abaci & Liber Quadratorum
fibonacci.summary: Developed additive recurrences whose 3-term proportion (z − x):(z − m) = m:x <-> x + m = z was already isolated as the Tenth Mean (3, 5, 8) in Nicomachus II.28.10–11 (`geometor/fibonacci`).

pacioli.name: Luca Pacioli
pacioli.summary: Built Renaissance proportion nomenclature, figurate progressions, and the contrast of rational superparticulars vs. the irrational Divine Proportion directly upon Boethius–Nicomachus (`geometor/pacioli`).

kepler.name: Johannes Kepler
kepler.summary: Unified the Quadrivium's geometry, music, and astronomy in Harmonices Mundi (1619), critiquing purely arithmetic Neo-Pythagorean number symbolism while fulfilling Nicomachus's harmonic cosmos through constructible polygons (`geometor/kepler`).

hoche.name: Richard Gottfried Hoche
hoche.role: Classical philologist & editor of the 1866 Teubner Greek text
hoche.summary: Edited both John Philoponus's Commentary on Nicomachus (1864–1867) and the standard critical Teubner edition Nicomachi Geraseni Pythagorei Introductionis Arithmeticae Libri II (Leipzig, 1866), establishing the canonical text and α-pebble diagrams.

friedlein.name: Gottfried Friedlein
friedlein.summary: Published the critical Teubner edition of Boethius's De Institutione Arithmetica Libri Duo and De Institutione Musica Libri Quinque (Leipzig, 1867) immediately following Hoche's 1866 Greek Nicomachus.

dooge.name: Martin Luther D'Ooge
dooge.role: Professor of Greek at the University of Michigan & first English translator of Nicomachus
dooge.summary: Completed the authoritative first English translation of Nicomachus's Introduction to Arithmetic (published posthumously in 1926 by Macmillan / University of Michigan Studies, Humanistic Series Vol. XVI, with studies by F. E. Robbins and L. C. Karpinski).

robbins.name: Frank Egleston Robbins & Louis Charles Karpinski
robbins.role: Co-authors of Studies in Greek Arithmetic (1926)
robbins.summary: Completed and annotated D'Ooge's 1926 Michigan edition with comprehensive philological, mathematical, and historical studies on Greek arithmetic, sources of Nicomachus, and medieval reception.

heath.name: Sir Thomas Little Heath
heath.summary: Provided standard modern mathematical analyses of Nicomachus's Introductio Arithmetica in A History of Greek Mathematics (1921, Vol. I, pp. 97–115) and The Thirteen Books of Euclid's Elements (`geometor/euclid`).
